name: Vim
summary: A modal text editor whose main loop coordinates character input and Ex commands over mutable buffers and windows, with Vim script, jobs, and channels extending the editor boundary.
scope: Ex command and Vim script execution

features.name: Modal buffer and window state
features.description: The fixed source enters a main editor loop, obtains typed input, and applies commands to buffers, windows, and undo state. Vim's user documentation describes Normal, Insert, and other modes as distinct interpretations of input.
benefits: Separates navigation and editing commands from inserted text
Keeps buffer, window, and undo state under one editor lifecycle
costs: Window, buffer, and undo mutations share the responsiveness of the main loop

features.name: Ex command and Vim9 execution boundary
features.description: The source parses and executes Ex command lines through do_cmdline and implements a separate Vim9 compilation and execution surface. The official help documents Ex commands and Vim9 script as programmable editor interfaces.
benefits: Provides both interactive command composition and reusable scripts
Allows language evolution while retaining the established Ex boundary
costs: Multiple command and script execution paths increase compatibility surface
Script errors and recursive command execution interact with editor state

features.name: Job and channel integration
features.description: Vim maintains channels and jobs alongside the editor loop, polls pending work, parses channel messages, and exposes callbacks and terminal buffers. The official job-control help describes asynchronous jobs and channel communication.
benefits: Lets scripts communicate with external processes without replacing editor state
Provides structured callbacks and message handling for plugins and tools
costs: Asynchronous callbacks add ordering and reentrancy obligations
External process and transport failures cross the editor boundary

mathematical_views.question: How do input characters and Ex commands transform mode, buffer, window, and undo state?
assumptions: Editor state includes the current mode, buffers, windows, cursor, and undo history
Input dispatch selects transitions based on the active mode and command parser
The view abstracts terminal timing and exact redraw implementation

mathematical_views.question: Which editor resources and external jobs are connected through channels and callbacks?
assumptions: Buffers and windows are mutable editor resources, while jobs and channels are external-process boundaries
Edges represent command, message, callback, or terminal-buffer interactions
The graph describes reachability and does not imply synchronous completion or safety

costs: Mode transitions must remain discoverable and correct

benefits: Interactive commands and scripts share editor operations
costs: Legacy and newer script semantics increase maintenance burden

benefits: External tools can participate in editor workflows
costs: Process lifecycle and callback ordering become editor concerns
